title: Harvard's Silicon Chip Writes DNA with Electricity, Opening Door to Cleaner Synthesis and Data Storage
summary:
Silicon chips revolutionized computing; now they're poised to transform biotechnology. In a study published in Nature Electronics, a Harvard-led team unveiled a chip that can synthesize 64 different DNA sequences simultaneously using an enzymatic, water-based process—a stark departure from the solvent-heavy chemical methods that dominate the industry.

The chip's surface contains 64 synthesis sites, each with two concentric ring electrodes. When activated, the inner electrode generates protons that lower the pH locally, triggering the deprotection step needed to add the next nucleotide. The outer electrode scavenges stray protons, confining the acidic zone to a single site. By cycling through this process, the chip independently builds 64 unique DNA strands up to 39 nucleotides long—a new high for parallel enzymatic synthesis.

'This was not originally a DNA synthesis chip,' explained Donhee Ham, the study's senior author. It began as a tool for recording neuronal activity, using precision current injection to permeabilize cell membranes. 'At a certain point, we wondered whether that same current control could be redirected from cells to molecules,' Ham said. After redesigning the electrodes, the team found it could localize pH for DNA writing. The result is a cleaner, potentially decentralized alternative to phosphoramidite chemistry, which relies on hazardous organic solvents and centralized facilities.

Beyond synthetic biology and diagnostics, the team demonstrated a proof-of-concept for DNA data storage. They encoded a 169-byte text into the 64 sequences, hinting at a future where massive archives are stored in DNA. 'DNA data storage asks DNA synthesis to operate at a scale far beyond today's needs,' said co-first author Woo-Bin Jung. 'If far more than 64 sequences can be synthesized in parallel, it could offer an environmentally friendly route toward writing DNA at very large scale.' While that vision remains distant, the chip marks a significant step toward sustainable, high-throughput enzymatic synthesis.
why_it_matters: This technology could democratize DNA synthesis, making it safer and more accessible worldwide, which would accelerate research in medicine, agriculture, and environmental science. As digital data grows exponentially, DNA data storage might become essential to reduce the energy and physical footprint of data centers, linking biology with computing for a more sustainable future.

background_read: Harvard University, founded in 1636 in Cambridge, Massachusetts, is a world-leading research institution whose scientists have contributed to everything from computers to medicine.
The dominant method of DNA synthesis, known as phosphoramidite chemistry, uses hazardous organic solvents and requires centralized, expensive facilities, limiting its widespread use.
The study appears in Nature Electronics, a peer-reviewed journal that publishes advances in electronic devices and systems.
Donhee Ham, the senior author, is a professor at Harvard's School of Engineering and Applied Sciences, known for his work on nanoelectronics and biointerfaces.

DNA data storage is a futuristic concept: a single gram of DNA can theoretically store hundreds of petabytes of data, making it an attractive option for archiving humanity's growing digital information.

perspectives.description: The chip's enzymatic, water-based process eliminates toxic chemicals, making DNA synthesis safer for lab workers and reducing hazardous waste. Its parallel design could bring DNA writing out of centralized factories and into smaller labs or clinics, speeding up diagnostic test development and personalized medicine.

However, the current 39-nucleotide strand length is far short of the thousands of nucleotides needed for many real-world applications, and scaling up the number of parallel sites remains a huge engineering challenge. Without careful regulation, cheaper DNA synthesis could also make it easier to create pathogens or other dangerous biological agents.

The pivot from neuroscience to DNA synthesis is a striking example of how fundamental tools can be repurposed across disciplines—a pattern common in breakthrough technologies. The chip's confinement of protons using concentric electrodes is a clever bit of electrochemical engineering, but its practical edge over other enzymatic methods still needs to be proven in real-world workflows.

Looking ahead, if researchers can increase both strand length and site count, such chips might one day sit on a biochemist's benchtop, writing custom genes on demand. In the longer run, linking many chips together could enable 'DNA printers' that archive entire libraries or even record human knowledge in a form that can last millennia.
